title: Fluxes of Generic Extreme-Mass-Ratio Inspirals with a Spinning Secondary
summary: Extreme mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs), comprising a stellar-mass compact object (CO) orbiting a supermassive black hole (BH), are key targets for future space-based gravitational-wave (GW) observatories. Incorporating the spin of the secondary body into waveform models not only enhances measurement precision but also offers insight into the spin distribution of stellar-mass objects. In this work, we construct the flux and waveform for an EMRI with a spinning secondary in a Kerr background under the linear-spin approximation. Using the radiative prescription (half-retarded minus half-advanced field), we derive orbit-averaged evolution equations for the fundamental constants of motion, including the energy, angular momentum, Carter-like constant, and the parallel spin component. This framework provides a tractable route to generating waveforms that incorporate the secondary spin, with the potential for further simplification in future work.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a method to include the spin of the smaller compact object in EMRI waveform models using linear-spin approximation and radiative prescriptions, improving waveform accuracy and measurability for future space-based gravitational-wave detections.
AI.motivation: To improve EMRI waveform models by incorporating the spin of the secondary compact object, which enhances measurement precision and provides insights into the spin distribution of stellar-mass objects.
AI.method: Constructing flux and waveform models for an EMRI with a spinning secondary in a Kerr background using the linear-spin approximation and employing the radiative prescription to derive orbit-averaged evolution equations for constants of motion.
AI.result: Developed a tractable framework that includes the secondary spin in EMRI waveforms, yielding evolution equations for energy, angular momentum, Carter-like constant, and parallel spin component, enabling improved waveform generation with potential simplifications in future work.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating the secondary object's spin via linear-spin approximation and radiative prescription offers a practical method to generate more accurate EMRI waveforms, enhancing parameter estimation capabilities for future gravitational-wave observatories.

title: Discovery of Bimodal Drift Rate Structure in FRB 20240114A: Evidence for Dual Emission Regions
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We report the discovery of bimodal structure in the drift rate distribution of upward-drifting burst clusters from the hyperactive repeating fast radio burst FRB 20240114A. Using unsupervised machine learning (UMAP dimensionality reduction combined with HDBSCAN density-based clustering) applied to 233 upward-drifting burst clusters from the FAST telescope dataset, we identify a distinct subpopulation of 45 burst clusters (Cluster C1) with mean drift rates 2.5x higher than typical upward-drifting burst clusters (245.6 vs 98.1 MHz/ms). Gaussian mixture modeling reveals strong evidence for bimodality (delta-BIC = 296.6), with clearly separated modes (Ashman's D = 2.70 > 2) and a statistically significant gap in the distribution (11.3 sigma). Crucially, we demonstrate that this bimodality persists when restricting the analysis to single-component (U1) burst clusters only (delta-BIC = 19.9, Ashman's D = 2.71), confirming that the result is not an artifact of combining single- and multi-component burst clusters with different drift rate definitions. The extreme-drift subpopulation also exhibits systematically lower peak frequencies (-7%), shorter durations (-29%), and distinct clustering in multi-dimensional feature space. These findings are suggestive of two spatially separated emission regions in the magnetosphere, each producing upward-drifting burst clusters with distinct physical characteristics, although confirmation requires observations from additional epochs and sources.

AI.tldr: Using machine learning on FRB 20240114A data, researchers discovered two distinct classes of upward-drifting burst clusters differing in drift rates and other features, suggesting two separate magnetospheric emission regions.
AI.motivation: To investigate the statistical properties and physical origins of upward-drifting burst clusters from the hyperactive repeating fast radio burst FRB 20240114A.
AI.method: Applied unsupervised machine learning techniques, specifically UMAP dimensionality reduction combined with HDBSCAN density-based clustering, on 233 upward-drifting burst clusters from the FAST telescope dataset, followed by Gaussian mixture modeling to test for bimodality.
AI.result: Identified a distinct subpopulation of burst clusters with drift rates 2.5 times higher than typical clusters, confirmed strong evidence for bimodality with statistically significant separation, and found associated differences in peak frequency and burst duration, supporting the hypothesis of two spatially separated emission regions.
AI.conclusion: The discovery of bimodal drift rate distribution in upward-drifting burst clusters from FRB 20240114A suggests the existence of two spatially separated emission regions in the magnetosphere with distinct physical properties.

title: Probing Kerr black hole in a uniform Bertotti-Robinson magnetic field through astrophysical quasi-periodic oscillations
summary: In this study, the behavior of high-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) is investigated around a Kerr black hole immersed in a uniform Bertotti-Robinson magnetic field. The motion of the test particle is analyzed by determining the geodesic equations and evaluating the corresponding orbital, radial, and vertical epicyclic frequencies. These fundamental frequencies are used to construct the theoretical framework of QPO models based on parametric and forced resonance mechanisms. Observational data obtained from several black hole X-ray binaries (GRO J1655-40, XTE J1550-564, XTE J1859+226, GRS 1915+105, H1743-322, M82~X-1, and Sgr~A$^{*}$) are used to constrain the black hole parameters through Bayesian inference and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses. For the X-ray binaries GRO J1655-40, GRS 1915+105, H1743-322, and M82~X-1, nonzero values of the dimensionless parameter $b=Bm$ are obtained at the $68\%$ confidence level within the framework of the parametric resonance model, while only upper bounds at the $90\%$ confidence level are obtained for the remaining sources. In contrast, in the case of the forced resonance model, only an upper bound at the $90\%$ confidence interval is obtained for the magnetic field parameter for all considered X-ray binary sources. The analysis indicates that the value of the magnetic field parameter is small but not negligible, producing minor modifications to particle dynamics and epicyclic frequencies. The influence of the magnetic field is further examined through the properties of the innermost stable circular orbit and the radiative properties of the thin accretion disk, including the energy flux and temperature profiles, within the allowed parameter range inferred from the MCMC analysis.

AI.tldr: This study models how a uniform magnetic field affects quasi-periodic oscillations near Kerr black holes, using observational data and advanced statistical methods to infer small but significant magnetic effects on particle orbits and disk characteristics around these black holes.
AI.motivation: To investigate the effects of a uniform Bertotti-Robinson magnetic field on high-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) around Kerr black holes, in order to better understand black hole parameters and particle dynamics in magnetized environments.
AI.method: Analyzed test particle motion via geodesic equations to calculate orbital and epicyclic frequencies; developed QPO models based on parametric and forced resonances; employed Bayesian inference and Markov Chain Monte Carlo analyses on observational data from multiple black hole X-ray binaries to constrain black hole and magnetic field parameters.
AI.result: Nonzero magnetic field parameter values were found for some X-ray binaries within parametric resonance models at 68% confidence, while forced resonance models yielded only upper bounds; magnetic fields slightly modify particle dynamics and epicyclic frequencies; the magnetic field's effect on the innermost stable circular orbit and thin disk radiative properties was characterized within inferred parameter ranges.
AI.conclusion: The presence of a weak but non-negligible magnetic field around Kerr black holes influences QPO behavior and associated particle dynamics, with measurable effects on disk properties, supporting the inclusion of magnetic fields in models of black hole accretion phenomena.

title: Spectral Hardness as the Primary Discriminator: Unveiling the Collapsar--Merger Boundary with a Gold-Standard Gamma-Ray Burst Sample
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures and 2 tables; accepted by APJ Letters
summary: In this Letter, we establish a robust, physically motivated classification method using a Support Vector Machine (SVM) trained on a "gold-standard" sample of 24 GRBs with spectroscopically confirmed progenitors (associated SNe or KNe). By isolating the prompt main spike to excise contamination from extended emission, we derive a quantitative classification index, I_SVM = 5.01 log_10 E_p,i - 1.25 log_10 E_iso - 0.34 log_10 T_90,z - 12.90 (units: keV, 10^52 erg, s). Events with I_SVM > 0 are classified as mergers. Analysis of the standardized classification weights reveals that the discriminative power of E_p,i is approximately 5 times that of T_90,z, while E_iso contributes a weight comparable to E_p,i. This quantitatively demonstrates that spectral hardness and energetics, rather than duration, are the primary physical signatures distinguishing mergers from collapsars. The derived boundary implies a stringent hardness ceiling for collapsars, while mergers are identified as outliers with excessive hardness relative to their energy budget. The classifier successfully identifies the nature of historic test cases, including the ultra-long GRB 111209A (collapsar) and the short GRB 050709 (merger), independent of instrumental eras. This tool paves the way for cleaning archival and future high-redshift GRB samples for precision cosmology.

AI.tldr: An SVM-based classifier using spectral and energetic parameters effectively differentiates GRB progenitors, prioritizing hardness and energy over duration, providing a reliable, physics-driven tool for classifying mergers versus collapsars.
AI.motivation: To establish a robust and physically motivated classification method to distinguish gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) based on their progenitors, addressing contamination in prompt emission data and improving the physical understanding of GRB classification.
AI.method: Developed a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier trained on a gold-standard sample of 24 GRBs with spectroscopically confirmed progenitors, using isolated prompt main spike emission to remove extended emission contamination. Derived a classification index (I_SVM) combining logarithmic transformations of spectral peak energy (E_p,i), isotropic energy (E_iso), and duration (T_90,z).
AI.result: The classifier distinguishes mergers (I_SVM > 0) from collapsars, revealing spectral hardness (E_p,i) and energetics (E_iso) as the dominant discriminants over burst duration (T_90,z). The method correctly identified historic GRBs with known progenitors and set a hardness ceiling for collapsars, identifying mergers as outliers in hardness.
AI.conclusion: Spectral hardness and energetics are the primary physical signatures differentiating GRB progenitors rather than duration, enabling a standardized, instrument-independent classification tool that improves accuracy in GRB categorization and facilitates precision cosmology with cleaned samples.

title: High-redshift physics from the acoustic scale
summary: We present a simplified and general description of the high-redshift information in acoustic scale measurements from the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure. The transverse distance interval between photon--baryon decoupling and a late epoch in the matter era provides an analytically tractable summary statistic thereof and a general diagnostic of the current tension between the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and the CMB. We show that this "matter-era distance excess" is unlikely to be explained by modified dynamics at low redshift. We then analytically derive the matter-era distance interval's sensitivity to new physics at high redshift, including nonstandard recombination, nonminimal dark matter dynamics, and spatial curvature; in particular, we explain how this observable represents a direct geometric measurement of (and underlies the current incompatibility with) neutrino masses. Finally, we demonstrate that phenomenological models of dynamical dark energy mediate the matter-era distance excess in a manner reliant on their unphysical, extrapolated behavior at high redshift. Invoking alternative explanations of the excess removes the CMB's contribution to the evidence for these models; the residual preference of around $1.7σ$ mostly derives from DESI's two lowest-redshift measurements of the Alcock--Paczynski distortion, without which it drops to $0.5 σ$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a simplified metric for high-redshift acoustic scale data that elucidates tensions between DESI and CMB measurements, revealing the geometric nature of neutrino mass constraints and questioning dark energy model interpretations based on extrapolated high-redshift behavior.
AI.motivation: To provide a simplified, general description of high-redshift information in acoustic scale measurements and address the tension between DESI and CMB observations.
AI.method: Develop an analytically tractable summary statistic based on the transverse distance interval between photon--baryon decoupling and a late matter era epoch; derive the sensitivity of this matter-era distance interval to different high-redshift physics and analyze implications for neutrino masses and dark energy models.
AI.result: The matter-era distance excess is unlikely explained by low-redshift modified dynamics; it serves as a direct geometric probe of high-redshift physics and neutrino masses; phenomenological dynamical dark energy models are shown to mediate the excess based on unphysical extrapolations, and removing the CMB's role reduces evidence for these models, with residual tension mainly from low-redshift DESI measurements.
AI.conclusion: The matter-era distance interval provides a robust, simplified approach to summarize high-redshift acoustic scale data, clarifies incompatibilities related to neutrino masses, challenges certain dark energy interpretations, and highlights the importance of low-redshift measurements in current cosmological tensions.

title: Supermassive Black Hole Winds in X-rays: SUBWAYS V. Properties of hot coronae in quasars at intermediate redshift
summary: We present the X-ray analysis of coronal properties in a statistically representative sample of 23 mostly radio-quiet AGN from the SUBWAYS campaign (SUpermassive Black holes Winds in XrAYs), focusing on quasars at redshifts $0.1 < z < 0.4 $ and bolometric luminosities $2 \times 10^{44} <L_{bol}(erg/s) < 2 \times 10^{46}$. The main aim of this work is to investigate the properties of the hot corona through the study of the hard X-ray band emission, including a proper treatment of the soft X-ray band. High-quality X-ray spectra from XMM-Newton, complemented by NuSTAR data extending up to 30-40 keV in the rest frame, are available for this sample. The soft X-ray band (0.3-2 keV) spectrum is best fitted by a warm corona model with a median temperature of 0.40 keV, and an optical depth in the range $τ$=20 - 40, consistent with previous results on lower luminosity sources. The hard X-ray band is well described using a hot corona model, with a median high-energy cut-off of 87 keV, at the lower end of the distribution of typical values found in Seyfert galaxies (100 - 200 keV). The derived median value of the optical depth ($τ$ = 1 - 5) suggests the presence of a moderately optically thick corona. Combining the SUBWAYS results with literature samples at low and high redshift, we assemble the largest sample to date of AGN with E$_{cut}$ and accretion parameter measurements, finding a significant anticorrelation of E$_{cut}$ with both $λ_{Edd}$ and $L_{bol}$ with the median E$_{cut}$ decreasing from 250 - 300 keV at low accretion rates and luminosities to 90 - 100 keV at high accretion rates and luminosities - consistent with enhanced coronal cooling, possibly driven by pair-production. These results favor cooler, optically thicker coronae in luminous AGN compared to those in lower-luminosity Seyfert galaxies.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes X-ray spectra of 23 quasars, finding their hot coronae to be cooler and more optically thick than those in Seyfert galaxies, with high-energy cut-offs decreasing as accretion rates and luminosities increase, suggesting enhanced coronal cooling.
AI.motivation: To investigate the properties of the hot corona in quasars by analyzing their hard X-ray emission, including a proper treatment of the soft X-ray band, to better understand coronal physics in luminous AGN.
AI.method: X-ray spectral analysis was conducted on a representative sample of 23 mostly radio-quiet AGN using high-quality XMM-Newton spectra complemented by NuSTAR data extending up to 30-40 keV. Both soft (0.3-2 keV) and hard X-ray bands were fitted using warm and hot corona models respectively.
AI.result: The soft X-ray band spectrum is best described by a warm corona with median temperature 0.40 keV and optical depth 20-40. The hard X-ray emission fits a hot corona model with median high-energy cut-off of 87 keV and optical depth 1-5. An anticorrelation was found between the cutoff energy and both Eddington ratio and bolometric luminosity, indicating cooler, optically thicker coronae at higher accretion rates and luminosities.
AI.conclusion: Luminous AGN host cooler and more optically thick coronae compared to lower-luminosity Seyfert galaxies, likely due to enhanced coronal cooling driven by pair-production, as evidenced by the decrease in high-energy cutoff with increasing accretion rate and luminosity.

title: TUNeS: Neural Emulation of Large-Scale Structure Across Redshifts
summary: In this work, we introduce TUNeS (Temporal UNet emulator for Structure formation), a neural network framework for accelerating N-body simulations by predicting the nonlinear evolution of the matter density field from an initial particle distribution. TUNeS employs a two-stage modeling strategy, combining particle-based inference with a density-field refinement on a regular grid, enabling accurate reconstruction of both large- and small-scale structures. The model is designed to operate across redshift, taking particle snapshots at arbitrary input redshifts and predicting density fields at arbitrary target redshifts. In this work, we evaluate its performance using simulations initialized at $z=100$, with predictions generated at multiple lower redshifts. Trained on only eight N-body simulations, TUNeS reproduces reference results with good agreement in both Gaussian and non-Gaussian statistics, including two-point correlations, one-point distributions, peak counts, and three-dimensional Minkowski functionals. In particular, at $k \simeq 1\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, the power spectrum error remains at the few-percent level. End-to-end inference from $256^3$ particles to a $256^3$ density grid can be completed in $\sim25\,\mathrm{second}$ on a single GPU. Thanks to its architectural design, the model naturally scales to larger particle numbers and larger volumes through particle batching and window-based refinement.

AI.tldr: TUNeS is a neural network framework accelerating N-body simulations by accurately predicting nonlinear matter density evolution from initial particles to density grids across redshifts, achieving fast, scalable, and precise results with minimal training data.
AI.motivation: Accelerate N-body simulations of matter density field evolution while maintaining accuracy across multiple scales and redshifts.
AI.method: TUNeS employs a two-stage neural network combining particle-based inference with density-field refinement on a grid, designed to predict nonlinear evolution of matter density from initial particle distributions across arbitrary redshifts.
AI.result: Trained on only eight simulations, TUNeS accurately reproduces both Gaussian and non-Gaussian statistical properties of the matter density field, with power spectrum errors at the few-percent level at relevant scales, and runs efficiently on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: TUNeS successfully enables fast and accurate nonlinear structure formation predictions across scales and redshifts, scalable to large particle counts and volumes, offering a significant speed-up over traditional N-body simulations.

title: Neutrinos and gamma rays from Seyfert galaxies constrain the properties of coronal turbulence
summary: The TeV neutrino signal observed by IceCube from the active galactic nucleus (AGN) NGC 1068 can probe its innermost coronal regions. If these neutrinos originate from hadrons accelerated within a magnetized turbulent corona, their intensity and spectrum depend on the turbulent magnetic field strength and turbulence coherence scale. The gamma rays accompanying neutrino production are absorbed in this optically thick environment, in a way that depends sensitively on the size of the corona. By a joint fit of the IceCube and Fermi-LAT observations, we translate the multimessenger signal from NGC 1068 and the tentative signal from NGC 7469 into quantitative constraints on coronal properties. NGC 1068, with a significant TeV neutrino excess, favors a compact, strongly magnetized corona with a large turbulence coherence length relative to the coronal size. NGC 7469, with two $\sim 100$ TeV neutrino events, points instead to a somewhat larger corona with much smaller coherence length and high magnetization, but a very small fraction of energy in non-thermal protons. We obtain the diffuse flux from a population of Seyfert galaxies identical to either NGC 1068 or NGC 7469. Finally, we consider a third scenario, motivated by the spectral break observed in the diffuse neutrino flux at tens of TeV, with coronal properties intermediate between the two point-source-inspired models. To enable detailed comparisons with the IceCube and electromagnetic observations, we release our model predictions in a GitHub repository.

AI.tldr: By jointly analyzing IceCube neutrino and Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data from AGNs NGC 1068 and NGC 7469, this study constrains their coronal magnetic turbulence properties, revealing distinct coronal characteristics linked to neutrino production, and models diffuse neutrino flux from Seyfert galaxies, offering predictions for further observational tests.
AI.motivation: To probe the innermost coronal regions of active galactic nuclei (AGN) through the TeV neutrino signals observed, and to understand the connection between neutrino production and coronal magnetic turbulence properties.
AI.method: Joint fitting of multimessenger data from IceCube (neutrinos) and Fermi-LAT (gamma rays) for AGNs NGC 1068 and NGC 7469; modeling neutrino and gamma-ray spectra accounting for magnetized turbulent coronal environments with varying magnetic field strengths, coherence lengths, and coronal sizes; and comparison to diffuse neutrino flux measurements.
AI.result: NGC 1068 favors a compact, strongly magnetized corona with a large turbulence coherence length, while NGC 7469 favors a larger corona with smaller coherence length and high magnetization but low non-thermal proton energy fraction. Diffuse neutrino flux from Seyfert galaxy populations modeled accordingly, with a third intermediate coronal property scenario explaining spectral breaks in observed diffuse neutrino flux. Model predictions publicly released for further comparison.
AI.conclusion: The study quantitatively constrains AGN coronal properties through multimessenger observations, demonstrating the role of magnetic turbulence parameters in neutrino and gamma-ray production, and provides a framework for interpreting diffuse neutrino flux and individual AGN contributions.

title: Gamma-Ray Bursts as an Independent High-Redshift Probe of Dark Energy
summary: Testing the $Λ$CDM model requires cosmological probes spanning the wide redshift interval between Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia, $z\lesssim2.9$) and the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB, $z\approx1100$). Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs), observed up to redshift $z=9.2$, offer the opportunity to explore this regime. Here, we investigate how many GRBs are needed to become a useful cosmological probe capable of independently testing deviations from $Λ$CDM suggested by the recent DESI BAO observations. We develop forecasts based on the two-dimensional X-ray and optical Dainotti relations, between the luminosity at the end of the plateau phase and its rest-frame duration. Using simulated GRB samples constructed from the observed population, we evaluate the constraining power of GRBs on cosmological parameters within the $w$CDM and $w_0w_a$CDM models, both independently and in combination with CMB observations. Our results show that GRB samples containing several tens to hundreds of well-characterized plateau can already approach the precision currently achieved by CMB measurements on the Dark Energy (DE) equation-of-state parameter $w$. Particularly, a sample of $\sim66$ optical GRBs can reach a precision $σ_w \approx 0.47$, comparable to that obtained from Planck within the $w$CDM framework. Such sample sizes are already attainable through Machine Learning techniques that double the number of GRBs using inferred redshifts. These forecasts indicate that future GRB observations, when combined with next-generation transient missions and improved statistical techniques, will provide an independent high-redshift probe of cosmic expansion and will play an important role in testing the robustness of potential Dynamical DE signals suggested by other cosmological datasets.

AI.tldr: This study forecasts that Gamma-Ray Bursts, using Dainotti relations and enhanced by Machine Learning, can independently constrain Dark Energy parameters with precision comparable to CMB data, offering a valuable high-redshift test of the $\Lambda$CDM model and its alternatives.
AI.motivation: To test the $\Lambda$CDM model across the redshift range between SNe Ia and CMB, utilizing Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) which reach higher redshifts, aiming to independently verify deviations from $\Lambda$CDM indicated by recent observations.
AI.method: Forecasts based on the two-dimensional X-ray and optical Dainotti relations were developed using simulated GRB samples derived from observed populations. The constraining power of GRBs on cosmological parameters was evaluated for $w$CDM and $w_0w_a$CDM models, both independently and combined with CMB data.
AI.result: GRB samples containing several tens to hundreds of well-characterized plateaus can approach the precision of current CMB measurements for the DE equation-of-state parameter $w$. Approximately 66 optical GRBs yield a precision $\sigma_w \approx 0.47$, comparable to Planck results within the $w$CDM framework. Machine Learning methods can increase sample sizes by inferring redshifts, making such datasets attainable.
AI.conclusion: Future GRB observations, combined with next-generation transient missions and advanced statistical techniques, will provide an independent high-redshift cosmological probe. They will play a crucial role in testing the robustness of potential Dynamical Dark Energy signals suggested by other datasets.

title: A systematic search for physical associations between fast radio bursts and astrophysical transients
summary: The physical origin of fast radio bursts (FRBs) remains an unsolved mystery in astrophysics, with the magnetar central engine model as the leading framework. Systematically searching for physical associations between FRBs and the energetic astrophysical transients (ATs) that form magnetars provides a critical test of this scenario, and key clues to FRB progenitors. We perform a systematic search for FRB-AT associations using a sample of 3765 unique FRBs, combining the second CHIME/FRB catalog with 124 additional localized FRBs with measured redshifts. We develop a 3D Bayesian inference framework that jointly incorporates angular separation, positional uncertainty, and redshift constraints to quantify the association probability of candidate pairs. Through spatial cross-matching, we identify 14 FRB-optical transient and 15 FRB-gamma-ray burst (GRB) candidate pairs. Our framework recovers the previously reported high-significance association between FRB 20180916B and AT 2020hur, with an association probability of 0.9998. For the proposed candidate FRB 20190309A and short GRB 060502B, our analysis yields an association probability of 0.83, which is insufficient to claim statistically significant association. No new statistically significant FRB-AT associations are found for all remaining candidates. Our work demonstrates that small angular separation alone is insufficient to confirm FRB-AT associations, and high-precision FRB localization is essential for definitive identification.

AI.tldr: This study develops a 3D Bayesian framework to assess associations between fast radio bursts and energetic astrophysical transients, confirming one known association but finding no new significant links, highlighting the necessity of high-precision FRB localization for definitive progenitor identification.
AI.motivation: To test the magnetar central engine model for the physical origin of fast radio bursts (FRBs) by systematically searching for associations between FRBs and energetic astrophysical transients (ATs) that form magnetars, which could provide key clues to FRB progenitors.
AI.method: A systematic search was conducted using a sample of 3765 unique FRBs by combining the CHIME/FRB catalog and additional localized FRBs with redshifts. A 3D Bayesian inference framework was developed to jointly incorporate angular separation, positional uncertainty, and redshift constraints to quantify association probabilities of candidate FRB-AT pairs.
AI.result: 14 FRB-optical transient and 15 FRB-gamma-ray burst candidate pairs were identified. The framework recovered the known high-significance association between FRB 20180916B and AT 2020hur with a probability of 0.9998. Another proposed association (FRB 20190309A and short GRB 060502B) had an association probability of 0.83, which was not statistically significant. No other statistically significant associations were found.
AI.conclusion: Small angular separation alone is inadequate to confirm FRB-AT associations. High-precision localization of FRBs is critical for definitive association identification, and this study provides a robust Bayesian tool for evaluating candidate associations to test progenitor models.

title: Beyond Linear Bias Expansions for AbacusSummit Halos at z = 8
summary: We study the non-Gaussianity of the large-scale clustering of high-redshift halos, seeking to assess which terms of standard bias expansions are needed to understand these highly biased populations. We find that the clustering can be well modeled with only linear and quadratic bias parameters while assuming a Gaussian underlying matter field. Our analysis focuses on AbacusSummit halos at redshift $z=8$. We work with halos of mass at least $1\times10^{11}h^{-1}M_\odot$ in boxes of side length $2h^{-1}$Gpc. Measurements of bias coefficients are made by fitting bias expansions to the halo power spectrum and bispectrum. Tidal bias is not detected with only a ~$0.1σ$ deviation from $0$, but we see a $17σ$ level detection for a bias term of the form $δ^2$. A bias term of the form $δ^3$ is weakly detected at the $1.3σ$ level. Nonlinear matter is also detected at a $1.3σ$ level. To test how bias evolves, we run one test at $z=5$. We use a mass threshold for halos that gives the same variance in the halo field as our $z=8$ sample. Bias is smaller at $z=5$ and a tidal bias is detected at the $1σ$ level. Bias coefficients at $z=5$ match a linear evolution of the $z=8$ bias coefficients to within $10\%$.

AI.tldr: The study shows that at z=8, large-scale clustering of massive halos can be modeled using linear and quadratic bias terms assuming Gaussian matter; tidal bias is negligible. Bias evolves to z=5 consistent with linear theory, simplifying modeling of high-redshift halo clustering.
AI.motivation: To understand which bias terms are necessary to model the large-scale clustering of highly biased, high-redshift halos.
AI.method: Fitting bias expansions to the halo power spectrum and bispectrum of AbacusSummit halos at redshift z=8, using halos with mass greater than 1x10^11 h^-1 Msun in large volume simulations; comparing bias coefficients and their evolution by also analyzing halos at z=5 with matched variance.
AI.result: Clustering can be well modeled using only linear and quadratic bias parameters assuming a Gaussian matter field; tidal bias was not significantly detected at z=8 but a delta^2 bias term was strongly detected; weak detection of delta^3 bias and nonlinear matter; at z=5 bias is smaller with a 1σ tidal bias detection, and bias evolution is consistent with linear theory within 10%.
AI.conclusion: High-redshift halo clustering is effectively described by linear and quadratic bias terms without requiring tidal bias at z=8, with bias evolution to z=5 consistent with linear evolution; this simplifies modeling of non-Gaussianity in these populations.

title: GRB 241030A: a bright afterglow challenging forward shock emission
summary: Gamma-Ray Burst GRB 241030A (z = 1.411) exhibited a bright afterglow (similar to GRB 221009A), detected across gamma-ray, X-ray, UV, and optical bands, providing a probe of GRB afterglow physics. We compiled multi-wavelength observations spanning from a minute to a week after the prompt emission, processing the data through a unified photometry pipeline. We analysed the observations both analytically and using Bayesian inference with two independent models. Our models assume that the afterglow emission arises from the strong forward shock of a laterally structured jet, with possible contributions from synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) scatterings. Our models reproduce X-ray to optical data, favouring a jet propagating into a constant-density interstellar medium, with a viewing angle within the jet core. However, both analyses require parameter values that are extreme compared to expectations from standard theory. In particular, our results imply extremely energetic jets despite regular prompt energy, leading to a very inefficient prompt emission. Furthermore, the jets are inefficient at accelerating particles, with low electron and magnetic energy fractions, leading to significant SSC emission. Our analyses indicate that the jets have large opening angles and propagate in high-density media. If the afterglow is indeed powered by radiation emitted behind a strong forward shock, our results place GRB 241030A within a sub-class of GRBs characterised by extreme kinetic energies, large jet opening angles, and very low prompt emission efficiencies, with strong SSC radiation. These predictions are difficult to reconcile with typical expectations from other GRBs. We therefore suggest that the afterglow of GRB 241030A is not solely powered by forward shock emission.

AI.tldr: GRB 241030A's afterglow shows extreme energetic jets with inefficient prompt emission and strong SSC radiation, deviating from typical GRB models and indicating additional emission mechanisms beyond the forward shock.
AI.motivation: To understand the afterglow physics and energy dynamics of GRB 241030A by leveraging multi-wavelength observations and advanced modeling techniques.
AI.method: Collected and processed multi-wavelength data from gamma-ray to optical bands spanning from minutes to a week post-burst. Analyzed the data both analytically and using Bayesian inference with two independent models assuming afterglow emission from a laterally structured jet's forward shock and possible SSC contributions.
AI.result: Models reproduce the observed data favoring a jet in a constant-density medium viewed within the jet core but require extreme parameter values such as very energetic jets, low electron and magnetic energy fractions, large jet opening angles, and high-density media. These conditions imply inefficient prompt emission and strong SSC radiation, inconsistent with typical GRB expectations.
AI.conclusion: GRB 241030A belongs to a rare subclass of GRBs exhibiting extreme kinetic energy, large jet angles, and low prompt efficiencies accompanied by strong SSC emission. Such features challenge the standard forward shock afterglow model, suggesting that the afterglow is not solely powered by forward shock emission.

title: Lensing in the Blue III: Weak Lensing Shape Catalogs of 30 Merging Galaxy Clusters
summary: We present the weak gravitational lensing dataset from the Super-pressure Balloon-Borne Imaging Telescope (SuperBIT), which imaged 30 galaxy clusters during its 45 night flight in April to May 2023. SuperBIT is a first-of-its-kind balloon-borne imaging telescope that achieved near diffraction-limited observations in near-space conditions above 98% of the Earth's atmosphere. We use the metacalibration algorithm to obtain calibrated galaxy shapes for our target clusters and several calibration fields, enabling unbiased reconstruction of the weak-lensing signal. We employ several diagnostics throughout the pipeline, including assessments of point-spread function (PSF) modeling residuals and their impact on weak-lensing measurements, as well as tests for correlations between galaxy shapes and measured galaxy and PSF properties. To assess the multiplicative shear bias of the pipeline, we analyze a parallel set of simulated images that incorporate the real observing conditions from the flight, including measured SuperBIT PSFs, observed sky backgrounds, and detector noise, yielding a bias of $(1.1 \pm 7.8)$~per~cent.

AI.tldr: SuperBIT, a novel balloon-borne telescope, imaged 30 galaxy clusters and applied metacalibration for weak lensing analysis, achieving near-space quality data with minimal shear bias, validating its potential for future astrophysical observations.
AI.motivation: To obtain high-quality weak gravitational lensing data of galaxy clusters under near-space observing conditions using a balloon-borne telescope.
AI.method: Utilized the SuperBIT balloon-borne imaging telescope to image 30 galaxy clusters, applying the metacalibration algorithm for galaxy shape measurement, along with multiple diagnostics including PSF residual assessments and correlation tests; validated the analysis pipeline through simulations replicating real observing conditions.
AI.result: Achieved near diffraction-limited imaging above 98% of Earth's atmosphere, successfully reconstructing unbiased weak-lensing signals with a measured multiplicative shear bias of (1.1 ± 7.8)%.
AI.conclusion: The SuperBIT platform and metacalibration pipeline enable robust weak gravitational lensing measurements in near-space conditions, demonstrating promising capabilities for future cosmological studies using balloon-borne telescopes.

title: Non-Markovian Cosmic-Ray Pitch-Angle Transport from Mirror Interactions
summary: Cosmic-ray pitch-angle transport in magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence is governed by the interplay between magnetic mirroring and gyroresonant scattering. We develop a guiding-center (GC) Langevin model with explicit mirror drift and gyroresonant diffusion to describe the pitch angle evolution. This model accurately captures our test-particle simulation results in three-dimensional MHD turbulence, driven both solenoidally and compressively. We find that magnetic mirroring can drive anomalous pitch-angle diffusion at large pitch angles (including $90^\circ$) with non-Markovian memory effects, which arises from trapping of particles in magnetic wells. Gyroresonant scattering controls the escape rate from these wells. Across $M_{\rm A}$, large-pitch-angle particles are jointly regulated by mirror trapping and gyroresonant escape, exhibiting a transition from anomalous to normal diffusive pitch-angle transport as scattering strengthens, whereas small-pitch-angle particles remain gyroresonance-dominated and diffusive throughout. The pitch angle transport is found to be dominated by the compressible perturbations with marginal influence from Alfvén modes. In compressible turbulence with realistic damping accounted for, transit time damping (TTD) treatment fully recovers mirror interactions.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a Langevin model incorporating magnetic mirroring and gyroresonant scattering to describe cosmic-ray pitch-angle transport in MHD turbulence, validated by simulations. It reveals anomalous diffusion at large pitch angles caused by mirror trapping, controlled by gyroresonant escape, and a transition to normal diffusion with stronger scattering. Compressible turbulence dominates transport, with transit time damping fully accounting for mirror effects.
AI.motivation: To understand the governing mechanisms of cosmic-ray pitch-angle transport in magnetohydrodynamic turbulence, particularly the roles of magnetic mirroring and gyroresonant scattering.
AI.method: Developing a guiding-center Langevin model incorporating explicit mirror drift and gyroresonant diffusion, validated by three-dimensional test-particle simulations in both solenoidal and compressive MHD turbulence.
AI.result: Magnetic mirroring induces anomalous pitch-angle diffusion with non-Markovian memory effects at large pitch angles due to particle trapping in magnetic wells, while gyroresonant scattering regulates particle escape. Large-pitch-angle transport transitions from anomalous to normal diffusion with stronger scattering, whereas small-pitch-angle transport remains diffusive and gyroresonance-dominated. Compressible perturbations dominate the transport, with negligible influence from Alfvén modes. Transit time damping recovers mirror interactions in compressible turbulence with realistic damping.
AI.conclusion: The guiding-center Langevin model effectively captures the complex pitch-angle transport dynamics in MHD turbulence, highlighting the interplay between magnetic mirroring and gyroresonant scattering, with compressible perturbations playing a dominant role and providing insight into the transition between anomalous and normal diffusive regimes.

title: A Non-parametric Method for the Inference of Halo Occupation Distributions
comment: 27 pages, 18 figures, 2 tables. Nearly-final version after referee report, comments welcome!
summary: The galaxy-halo connection traces processes by which galaxies form and evolve. The halo occupation distribution (HOD) describes the relationship between galaxies and their host dark matter haloes. Measurements of the galaxy two-point correlation function (2PCF) allow us to extract information about the HODs of observed galaxy samples. Several parametric HOD models have been proposed in the literature, but the choice of parameterization restricts the space of possible HODs. To resolve this issue, we introduce a non-parametric HOD fitting method in which we train an emulator to learn the mappings among the galaxy 2PCF, physical properties used to select galaxy samples, and the HOD, all obtained from simulated past lightcones constructed with the Santa Cruz semi-analytic models. Implementing this emulator within a likelihood analysis framework, we derive constraints on the HOD of a galaxy sample when provided with a measurement of its 2PCF. Using the emulator to accelerate likelihood evaluations, we test the non-parametric HOD approach on a set of 2PCFs for mock galaxy samples drawn from the TNG100-1 simulation and selected above threshold values of stellar mass and star formation rate. Our framework is able to recover TNG100-1 HODs within 0.2 dex. We use the TNG100-1 mocks to tune the reported uncertainties to estimate those expected in the analysis of observations. Comparing to parametric HOD modeling routines applied to the same mock galaxy samples, our approach consistently infers the HOD with comparable or greater precision and accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a non-parametric method using an emulator and likelihood analysis to infer the halo occupation distribution from galaxy 2PCF data, achieving improved accuracy over traditional parametric models.
AI.motivation: Parametric HOD models limit the exploration of possible halo occupation distributions, motivating the need for a more flexible, non-parametric approach to better extract galaxy-halo relationships.
AI.method: A non-parametric HOD fitting method was developed using a trained emulator that learns mappings between galaxy 2PCF, galaxy sample properties, and HOD from simulated datasets, embedded within a likelihood analysis framework.
AI.result: The non-parametric emulator-based method accurately recovers HODs from mock galaxy samples with 0.2 dex precision, consistently outperforming or matching parametric methods in accuracy and precision.
AI.conclusion: By using a non-parametric emulator approach integrated in a likelihood framework, the study provides a more flexible and precise method to infer HODs from galaxy 2PCF measurements, overcoming limitations of parametric HOD models.

title: GRB 240205B: A Reverse Shock Detected in Rapid Response Radio Observations
summary: Here we present broadband radio modeling of GRB 240205B, using observations with the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) and the South African MeerKAT radio telescope. Our observations include an automatically triggered early-time ATCA observation that began approximately 13 minutes after the gamma-ray signal and continued for 12 hours, resulting in the earliest detected GRB radio afterglow to date at about 35 minutes post-burst. Following this initial detection, we conducted an extensive radio follow-up campaign for more than 5 months. Although the observations beyond one day post-burst are well described by a standard forward shock model, the observation before one day post-bust reveals an additional synchrotron component, which can be explained as the reverse shock. This component would have been missed without the automated ATCA rapid-response trigger. We find that a combined reverse and forward shock model in a stellar wind medium best describes the radio afterglow. We constrain the spectral breaks due to synchrotron self-absorption and the minimum electron energy, and we use the light-curve peaks to constrain the microphysical parameters. We put GRB 240205B in the context of the growing sample of GRBs with radio detections in the first hours after the gamma-ray trigger. Using our rapid response observation, we estimate the highest model independent constraint on a GRB minimum bulk Lorentz factor of around 100 at about 35 minutes post burst. We also discuss future prospects of detecting similar long GRBs at centimeter wavelengths, as well as potential improvements to future strategies for targeting their radio afterglows.

AI.tldr: This study presents the earliest radio afterglow detection of GRB 240205B using rapid-response ATCA observations, revealing both reverse and forward shock emissions, constraining physical parameters, and demonstrating the value of early radio monitoring for GRB characterization.
AI.motivation: To study the early-time radio afterglow of GRB 240205B with rapid-response observations, aiming to detect and characterize both forward and reverse shock components and improve understanding of GRB dynamics.
AI.method: Broadband radio observations were conducted using the ATCA and MeerKAT telescopes, including an automated rapid-trigger ATCA observation starting ~13 minutes post-burst and continuing for 12 hours, followed by a 5-month follow-up campaign; data were modeled using combined forward and reverse shock synchrotron emission in a stellar wind medium.
AI.result: The early-time radio afterglow showed both forward and reverse shock components, with the reverse shock detectable only due to early rapid response; spectral breaks and microphysical parameters were constrained, and a minimum bulk Lorentz factor of ~100 at 35 minutes post-burst was estimated.
AI.conclusion: Rapid-response radio observations enable detection of reverse shock components in GRB afterglows, allowing better parameter constraints; GRB 240205B's radio afterglow is best explained by a combined shock model in a stellar wind environment, with implications for future GRB detection strategies at centimeter wavelengths.

title: Primordial black holes and the velocity acoustic oscillations features in 21 cm signals from the cosmic Dark Ages
comment: 17 pages, 14 figures, accepted for publication in PRD
summary: Astrophysical luminous objects such as the first stars have not yet formed in the Dark Ages. However, primordial black holes (PBHs) always exist throughout cosmic history since the inflation epoch. During the Dark Ages, PBHs may accrete the ambient gas and release radiation like astrophysical luminous objects, change the cosmic radiation field, the thermal status of the intergalactic medium (IGM), and the hydrogen spin temperature. The accretion rate is modulated by the relic supersonic relative streaming velocities between dark matter (DM) and baryons, imprinting Velocity Acoustic Oscillations (VAOs) features in the 21 cm power spectrum. Such VAOs features could be a promising probe for detecting the PBHs in Dark Ages. We find that even if PBHs comprise only a small fraction of DM, they can generate VAOs wiggles with a relative amplitude up to about 30% in Dark Ages. For example, for PBHs with a mass at recombination of 200 solar masses and mass fraction in the total DM f_PBH,rec around 1e-13 at the recombination era, VAOs features appear at redshift around 20; if f_PBH,rec is around 3e-10, then VAOs features could appear as early as redshift around 40. Moreover, the redshift evolution of the VAOs features exhibits clearly separated stages dominated by inhomogeneous Ly-alpha scattering, and inhomogeneous X-ray heating, respectively. It reflects the characteristics of PBHs (mass and fraction in total DM) and their interactions with the IGM. We also estimate that, the VAOs wiggles at redshift around 20 are detectable for the upcoming SKA-low AA*, while wiggles at redshift around 40 are detectable for an hypothetic lunar surface-based interferometer array in the future.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that primordial black holes can imprint detectable Velocity Acoustic Oscillations in 21 cm signals during the Dark Ages, serving as a promising probe for PBHs' existence and characteristics.
AI.motivation: Primordial black holes (PBHs) may influence cosmic conditions during the Dark Ages despite the absence of luminous astrophysical objects, providing a unique probe for PBH detection.
AI.method: The study analyzes how PBHs accrete gas and emit radiation, modulated by relic supersonic streaming velocities between dark matter and baryons, imprinting Velocity Acoustic Oscillations (VAOs) in the 21 cm power spectrum across redshifts.
AI.result: PBHs even in small fractions of dark matter can induce VAO wiggles with up to 30% relative amplitude, with features appearing at redshifts ~20 to ~40 depending on PBH mass fraction. The VAO evolution reveals stages dominated by Ly-alpha scattering and X-ray heating, reflecting PBH properties and interactions with the intergalactic medium. Detectability is forecasted for SKA-low AA* and future lunar interferometers.
AI.conclusion: VAOs in the 21 cm power spectrum provide a sensitive signature of PBHs in the Dark Ages, enabling detection of small PBH fractions and offering insight into their properties and cosmic impacts before the first stars formed.

title: G objects as Primordial Black Hole-Neutron Star Remnants: Population Modeling and Multi-Wavelength Observables
summary: The nature of the so-called G objects orbiting the Galactic Center remains unresolved. These sources exhibit compact Br$γ$ emission, extreme infrared colors, and remarkable dynamical stability through close passages to the central supermassive black hole, challenging conventional interpretations as stars or unbound gas clouds. We investigate the hypothesis that G objects are the remnants of neutron stars that have been converted into low-mass black holes through the capture of primordial black holes, a viable dark-matter candidate. We construct a population-level framework linking the abundance and spatial distribution of these remnants to the neutron-star population, the inner dark-matter density profile, and the primordial black-hole mass and abundance. Within this framework, the observed G-object population and the long-standing deficit of ordinary radio pulsars in the Galactic Center emerge as complementary consequences of the same conversion process. We further identify a suite of observational signatures-across infrared, radio, X-ray, and microlensing channels-that render this scenario empirically testable and distinguishable from stellar-envelope models. Our results show that G objects can act as sensitive probes of compact-object capture physics and of dark matter on sub-galactic scales.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that G objects near the Galactic Center are neutron stars turned low-mass black holes by primordial black hole capture, offering a unified explanation for their properties and pulsar deficits, and outlines observational tests for this scenario.
AI.motivation: The nature of G objects orbiting the Galactic Center is unresolved due to their unusual emission properties and stability, defying conventional star or gas cloud models.
AI.method: Constructed a population-level framework linking G objects to neutron star remnants converted into low-mass black holes via primordial black hole capture, incorporating factors like neutron-star population, dark-matter density profile, and primordial black-hole parameters.
AI.result: The framework explains the observed G-object population and the deficit of radio pulsars as outcomes of the same conversion process and identifies multiple observational signatures to empirically test this hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: G objects can be interpreted as neutron star remnants converted by primordial black hole capture, serving as probes of compact-object capture physics and dark matter on sub-galactic scales, distinguishable from other stellar-envelope models.

title: A calibration-free null test from anisotropic BAO
summary: Baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) analyses usually report the anisotropic shift parameters $α_\perp(z)$ and $α_\parallel(z)$ relative to a fiducial cosmology, and these quantities are primarily used for cosmological parameter inference. Here we show that they can also be used to construct a direct internal consistency test of the background geometry. In particular, we derive a new null test of flat Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) geometry written entirely in terms of the reported BAO shift parameters. The test is calibration free: the sound-horizon ratio $r_{\rm d}/r^{\rm fid}_{\rm d}$ cancels identically, so the relation is independent of the absolute BAO scale. We also derive a calibration-free reconstruction of the deceleration parameter $q(z)$ from the radial BAO sector. Applying these results to anisotropic DESI DR2 BAO measurements, we find no evidence for a breakdown of the flat-FLRW distance relation within current uncertainties. Our results show that anisotropic BAO measurements already provide a nontrivial internal geometric consistency test before performing any model fit.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a calibration-free null test of flat FLRW geometry using anisotropic BAO shift parameters and confirms consistency with flat geometry in DESI DR2 data without model fitting.
AI.motivation: To provide an internal consistency test of the background cosmological geometry using anisotropic BAO data without reliance on absolute calibration.
AI.method: Derived a new null test of flat FLRW geometry based solely on BAO anisotropic shift parameters, eliminating dependence on the BAO scale by canceling the sound-horizon ratio; also constructed a calibration-free reconstruction of the deceleration parameter from radial BAO measurements.
AI.result: Applied the test to DESI DR2 anisotropic BAO data and found no deviation from flat FLRW distance relations within current measurement uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic BAO measurements can be used as a calibration-independent internal consistency check of flat FLRW geometry, providing a nontrivial geometric test prior to cosmological model fitting.

title: Half-wave-plate non idealities propagated to component separated CMB $B$-modes
summary: We assess the impact of non-ideal, continuously rotating half-wave plates (HWPs) on cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization measurements targeting large angular scale signal. Such hardware solutions are used in or planned for multiple modern CMB efforts, both ground-based, for instance, small aperture telescopes of Simons Observatory or satellite borne, such as LiteBIRD. Using a frequency-dependent parametric model based on the Mueller matrix formalism, we characterize the induced mixing of Stokes parameters. Through end-to-end simulations, we propagate these effects from time-ordered data to cosmology via map-making and component-separation stages, quantifying their impact on the $B$-modes power spectrum and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, $r$. Our analysis shows that neglecting the frequency dependence of a three-layer HWP gives rise to significant polarization leakage, biases foreground spectral parameters, and leads to residual contamination in the recovered CMB maps. To mitigate these effects, we investigate multiple analysis strategies progressively incorporating a more complete description of the instrumental response. At the map-making level, this requires generalizing the standard pointing matrix to account for the full time- and frequency-dependent instrumental response. We find that standard HWP models, reduce the biases only down to $r \sim 10^{-2}$, while a more advanced approach based on a generalization of both map-making and component separation, implemented using JAX, can suppress it down to $r \sim 7 \times 10^{-4}$. Finally, we extend this approach to a time-domain component-separation, enabling a statistically consistent treatment of instrumental response in the presence of time-domain features. We demonstrate its feasibility and validate it by performing a full end-to-end analysis, recovering results in good agreement with the map-based ones.

AI.tldr: This paper models and simulates the impact of realistic HWPs on CMB polarization measurements, showing that advanced analysis methods can significantly reduce biases in B-mode detection down to r ~ 7×10^-4, improving cosmological parameter estimation.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify how non-ideal, continuously rotating half-wave plates (HWPs) affect large angular scale CMB polarization measurements, crucial for improving detection of primordial gravitational waves through B-modes.
AI.method: Used a frequency-dependent parametric Mueller matrix model for HWPs, conducted end-to-end simulations propagating effects from time-ordered data through map-making and component separation, and developed progressively advanced analysis strategies including generalized pointing matrices and time-domain component separation implemented with JAX.
AI.result: Neglecting frequency dependence in three-layer HWPs causes significant polarization leakage and biases in foreground parameters, leading to residual contamination in CMB maps. Standard HWP models mitigate biases only to r ~ 10^-2, whereas advanced methods reduce biases to r ~ 7×10^-4, validated by consistent end-to-end analysis results.
AI.conclusion: A sophisticated modeling and analysis framework that incorporates frequency- and time-dependent instrumental responses of HWPs is essential to minimize biases in CMB B-mode measurements, enabling more accurate constraints on the tensor-to-scalar ratio r.
